name: Promethium

discovery.discoverer: Jacob A. Marinsky, Lawrence E. Glendenin & Charles D. Coryell

occurrence: Essentially absent in nature (all isotopes radioactive with short half-lives); produced artificially as a nuclear fission by-product.
majorUses: Historically used in self-luminous paint and betavoltaic 'nuclear batteries'
safetyNotes: Radioactive; handled only in shielded, controlled research and industrial settings.
notableCharacteristics: Named after Prometheus, the Greek Titan who stole fire for humanity — a nod to both the promise and the danger of harnessing nuclear science.
ncertRelevance: only lanthanide with no stable isotopes
whyHere: Promethium sits in a nuclear 'valley of instability' where every isotope is radioactive, making it — alongside technetium — one of only two elements below bismuth with no stable form at all, despite otherwise fitting neatly among its lanthanide neighbours.
didYouKnow: Promethium was the last of the naturally-occurring-mass-range elements to be discovered, only identified in 1945 by chemists sifting through the fission products of a nuclear reactor.
genZNote: Named after the guy who stole fire from the gods. Also the periodic table's reminder that not every gap gets filled naturally.
